title: World Time Zone Map: Zones and Offsets Live
description: Explore the world's time zones on the World Time Zone Map — coloured bands, UTC offsets and the political kinks straightened nowhere. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, China spans five geographic zones' worth of longitude yet keeps one time (UTC+8) — on the map it is a single colour from Kashgar to Shanghai, the widest kink in the system.
quick_answer: The World Time Zone Map shows the Earth's time zones as they are — coloured bands with UTC offsets, bent by borders and politics, not by longitude. Explore the map to read any region's zone and offset — and why the tidy school diagram survives nowhere.

Why does Spain keep Berlin's hour? Why is Nepal 15 minutes off India? The map raises the questions the articles answer.
Half-hour and quarter-hour zones (India, Iran, Nepal, the Chatham Islands) stand out once the bands are coloured.
Spain sits at London's longitude but keeps UTC+1 (a 1940 political choice aligned with Berlin) — solar noon in Galicia can fall near 14:30 by the clock in summer.
Kiribati pulled the line east around its islands in 1995, becoming the first country to greet the new day (UTC+14) — the map's easternmost bulge is that decision.

faq: Are the coloured areas exact political boundaries?
They show the standard published zone boundaries at map scale — authoritative for orientation. Border hamlets occasionally keep a neighbour's time informally; official IANA data governs conversion.
Does the offset update for daylight saving?
The map's context is date-aware where it displays current times; the safe habit is to convert specific dates with the Time Zone Converter, which applies the rules.
History: many zones were set from capital-city solar time before standardisation (Mumbai's legacy) or as political compromises (Nepal's +5:45 sets it apart from India deliberately).
Why does France appear to have twelve time zones?
Metropolitan France keeps one; its overseas territories — from French Guiana to New Caledonia — span the globe and keep their own, totalling twelve. The map colours them all.
Is an IANA zone better than a fixed offset?
Yes — a name like America/New_York carries the rule history (past and future DST changes); a raw −5 breaks twice a year. Store names, not numbers.
Why 24 zones in theory but more in practice?
Longitude suggests 24; politics, geography and history deliver ~38 distinct offsets today. The map is the practice.
Ships run on nautical time (by longitude band) and often switch to the destination's zone — the map's ocean bands are the nautical skeleton.
